readerTitle: Not every failure teaches the same lesson
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Amy Edmondson의 실패 분류, HBR 2011 / Right Kind of Wrong 2023) + 가상 사례 (카페 브런치, 일정 관리 앱)
insight: 실패에서 교훈을 찾기 전에 먼저 '어떤 종류의 실패였나'를 묻는다. 종류마다 맞는 대응이 다르다.
misconception: 실패는 모두 같은 방식으로 다루면 된다. 누군가의 잘못을 찾아 고치거나, 반대로 모든 실패를 '좋은 배움'으로 포장하면 된다.

sources.text: Edmondson, A. C. (2011). Strategies for Learning from Failure. Harvard Business Review, April 2011.
Edmondson, A. C. (2023). Right Kind of Wrong: The Science of Failing Well. Atria Books.
카페와 앱 사례의 모든 수치와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '비난받아 마땅한 실패 2~5%, 실제로 비난받는 실패 70~90%'는 Edmondson(2011, HBR)에서 임원들에게 물었을 때 나온 답변 범위로 소개됩니다. 엄밀한 통계 조사가 아니라 임원들의 추정이라는 점을 카드에 밝혔습니다. 게시 전 원문 문구를 다시 확인하세요.
basic / complex / intelligent 세 분류는 Edmondson의 2023년 책 용어입니다. 2011년 HBR 글은 preventable / complex / intelligent로 나눕니다. 카드에서는 'basic'을 쓰고 'preventable'과 같은 뜻으로 풀었습니다. 용어를 다시 확인하세요.
'지능적 실패'의 조건(새로운 영역, 분명한 가설, 가능한 한 작은 규모, 기회가 있음)은 Edmondson 책의 기준을 요약한 것입니다. 원문 기준(4가지)과 표현을 대조하세요.

cards.title: Three things went wrong at brunch. Only one was a mistake.
body: A neighborhood café launches weekend brunch. By noon, the hollandaise has run out, the line is out the door, and the new kimchi pancake has sold four plates.
The owner wants to know what went wrong. The trouble is, the answer is three different answers.

image.label: Busy café brunch with three small trouble spots
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트 스타일의 동네 카페 브런치 장면. 세 곳에 작은 말풍선 아이콘: 빈 소스 냄비, 문밖까지 늘어선 줄, 거의 손대지 않은 새 메뉴 접시. 실제 브랜드 로고나 간판은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Monday morning review
body: You own the café. Brunch brought in less than you hoped, and the team looks tense. You sit down together on Monday.

options.text: Decide brunch doesn't work here and drop it
options.feedback: Quick and decisive, but you'd throw away a launch that may have failed for fixable reasons, and learn nothing about which part actually broke.

options.text: Add stricter rules and checklists for everything
options.feedback: Checklists fix some problems well. But a rule can't tell you whether customers want a kimchi pancake, and too many rules slow down the next new idea.

options.text: Pull apart what went wrong and handle each problem differently
options.feedback: Slower on Monday, but each problem gets the fix it needs. The next cards show why this matters.

cards.title: Same morning, three different stories.

breakdown.label: Hollandaise ran out
breakdown.detail: The prep list said two batches. The second one was skipped.

breakdown.label: Waits at the door
breakdown.detail: New tablet ordering, two new servers and a surprise tour group, all at once

breakdown.label: Kimchi pancake
breakdown.detail: A brand-new dish, tried for one day

cards.callout: One known step skipped. One pile-up of small things. One honest experiment.

cards.title: Three kinds of failure
body: Harvard professor Amy Edmondson sorts failures by cause. **Basic failures** happen when there's a known right way, and it isn't followed. **Complex failures** happen when several small things line up in a system with many moving parts. **Intelligent failures** are thoughtful tries in new territory that don't work out.
**Learning from failure** starts with naming which kind it was. The lesson, and the fix, depend on the answer.

image.label: Three-part scale: basic, complex, intelligent failure
image.brief: 가로로 긴 스펙트럼 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Basic' (체크리스트 아이콘), 가운데 'Complex' (얽힌 톱니바퀴 아이콘), 오른쪽 'Intelligent' (실험용 플라스크 아이콘). 왼쪽은 '고쳐야 할 것', 오른쪽은 '배울 것'이라는 느낌으로 색을 점점 바꿈.

cards.title: Most failures get blamed. Few deserve it.
body: Edmondson asked executives two questions. How many failures in your company are truly someone's fault? And how many are treated that way? Their estimates, reported in a 2011 article:

breakdown.label: Truly blameworthy
breakdown.detail: Executives' estimate of failures that really were someone's fault

breakdown.label: Treated as blameworthy
breakdown.detail: Executives' estimate of failures handled as someone's fault

cards.callout: When every failure is blamed, people hide problems, and nobody learns from any of them.

cards.title: Different failures need different fixes.
body: Back at the café, each problem gets its own response:
list: **Basic:** fix the process. A prep checklist with a second check before opening.
**Complex:** reduce the pile-up. Don't launch new tablets and new staff on the same busy weekend.
**Intelligent:** keep the lesson. Four plates says something about price, name or placement. Test one change next week.
cards.callout: Punish an intelligent failure and people stop trying new things.
cards.softwareNote: The same split works for software teams. A skipped release check is basic. An outage from a traffic spike plus a new deploy is complex. A feature test nobody used is intelligent.

cards.title: Calling it "intelligent" doesn't make it so.
body: A failure earns that label only if the territory was truly new, you had a clear guess about what would happen, and you kept the try as small as you reasonably could. A full menu relaunch with no small test first is an expensive gamble, not an experiment.
Hindsight also makes causes look obvious. Before you try something new, write down what you expect. Afterward, you can compare instead of guess.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Last month your team offered a new paid add-on to 5% of users for two weeks. Almost nobody bought it.
The same month, the checkout page showed the wrong price for three days. A standard step, checking prices before each release, was skipped.
How should the review handle these?

options.text: Treat both as learning moments. No changes, no blame
options.feedback: Good for morale, but the price error was a basic failure. Without a process fix, it will happen again.

options.text: Fix the release checklist, and write up what the add-on test taught before designing the next one
options.feedback: Each failure gets a matching response: a process fix for the skipped step, and a recorded lesson for the small, well-run experiment.

options.text: Hold both teams accountable for missing their targets
options.feedback: It feels fair, but it treats a small test like a mistake. Next time, the team may skip experiments or hide weak results.

cards.title: Before asking what you learned, ask what kind of failure it was.
body: Basic failures need better processes. Complex ones need less pile-up. Intelligent ones need to be kept small, written down and built on.
**Try it today:** pick your last setback. Label it basic, complex or intelligent. Then write one fix that matches the label.
